[IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p40/r3] IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB, d. 392 · author | holds | Ibn Jinnī interprets the indefinite reading as humble obedience: the worshippers accept whatever straight guidance God grants, whether little or much, and promise to follow it.
[IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB:v1p40/r4] IBNJINNI-MUHTASAB, d. 392 · author | holds | He also hears an ongoing plea in the indefinite form: ‘keep guiding us’; the result is a straight path, expressed through an abstract description that becomes a concrete, exemplary person in his poetic analogies.
[SULAMI:v1p38#2/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | The prayer asks God to turn hearts toward Him and direct intentions before Him, guiding from Himself to Himself without severance from what is for Him.
[SULAMI:v1p38#2/r10] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | The requested path begins from God and ends at Him.
[SULAMI:v1p38#2/r11] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | It asks God to dispel the darkness of one's states so hidden realities may be seen steadily.
[SULAMI:v1p38#2/r12] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | One interpretation asks for self-effacement from the path, lest the traveler be trodden by it.
[SULAMI:v1p38#2/r13] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | The servant asks that concern with the path and steadfastness not distract from God Himself.
[SULAMI:v1p38#2/r14] SULAMI, d. 412 · أبو عثمان | reports | Guidance means being directed to use the Prophetic practices when fulfilling obligations.
[SULAMI:v1p38#2/r15] SULAMI, d. 412 · فضيل بن عياض | reports | He identifies the straight path with pilgrimage and the recipients of favor with prophets and saints; Jews and Christians are excluded, citing the prohibition on approaching the Sacred Mosque (9:28). | mentions 9:28
[SULAMI:v1p38#2/r16] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | The prayer seeks God's guidance against Satan, who vowed to sit on His straight path (7:16). | mentions 7:16
[SULAMI:v1p38#2/r17] SULAMI, d. 412 · أبو حفص النيسابوري | reports | The straight path is neediness before God; the poor person has nothing to present to the Rich but poverty.
[SULAMI:v1p38#2/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Seekers ask for guidance to paths of gnosis so they can serve steadily.
[SULAMI:v1p38#2/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Believers ask to see the path of guidance and stand firm in God's oneness.
[SULAMI:v1p38#2/r4] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Knowers ask for the path of intimacy so they may rejoice in nearness.
[SULAMI:v1p38#2/r5] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | Guidance from God to God bypasses the intermediary stations and struggles.
[SULAMI:v1p38#2/r6] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | One seeks annihilation of one's attributes as the way to God's eternal attributes.
[SULAMI:v1p38#2/r7] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | The prayer asks God to remove heedlessness from the route to His pleasure.
[SULAMI:v1p38#2/r8] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | It asks for direct witnessing after proof, so one may stand in love for God's will within oneself.
[SULAMI:v1p38#2/r9] SULAMI, d. 412 · بعضهم | reports | It asks for guidance to true knowledge under God's own care, ending in the annihilation of self-attributes in Him.
[SULAMI:v1p41/r1] SULAMI, d. 412 · سهل بن عبد الله | reports | Guidance is God's help in finding the way to Him.
[SULAMI:v1p41/r2] SULAMI, d. 412 · author | holds | Repeatedly asking for guidance seeks an increase even for someone already guided, as God says He increases guidance for those already guided (47:17). | mentions 47:17
[SULAMI:v1p41/r3] SULAMI, d. 412 · الجنيد | reports | The seekers ask to escape bewilderment before eternal attributes and to be guided to the qualities of servanthood, lest they be absorbed in witnessing God's eternal attributes.
[THALABI:v1p118#2/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · علي بن أبي طالب | reports | Ali and Ubayy understand the plea as asking to remain guided, like telling an eater to eat or a reader to continue reading.
[THALABI:v1p118#2/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddī and Muqātil gloss ihdinā as guide us to the path.
[THALABI:v1p118#2/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · الحسن بن الفضل | reports | One Qurʾanic sense of guidance is calling and clarification, as in the Prophet guiding to a straight path and each people having a guide. | mentions 42:52, 13:7
[THALABI:v1p118#2/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · الحسن بن الفضل | reports | A second sense is enabling and directing by God, as in verses saying God guides or misguides whom He wills and that the Prophet cannot guide whom he loves. | mentions 16:93, 28:56
[THALABI:v1p118#2/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The straight path is a clear, level road; verses by ʿĀmir ibn al-Ṭufayl and Jarīr illustrate the term.
[THALABI:v1p119/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · author | holds | The original form of ṣirāṭ is with sīn, reflecting the idea that the road swallows passersby; Ibn ʿAbbās read it this way, as did Ibn Kathīr and Yaʿqūb through cited routes.
[THALABI:v1p119/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو العالية الرياحي | reports | Abū al-ʿĀliya says it is the path of the Prophet and his two companions.
[THALABI:v1p119/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو حمدون عن الكسائي | reports | One transmitted reading gives ṣirāṭ an imāla-like sīn pronunciation (ishmām).
[THALABI:v1p119/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو حمدون عن سليم عن حمزة | reports | A transmitted reading pronounces the sīn as zāy.
[THALABI:v1p119/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · حمزة | reports | Hamza in most transmissions and al-Kisāʾī in two routes use ishām of zāy.
[THALABI:v1p119/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · author | reports | The remaining canonical readers pronounce ṣād.
[THALABI:v1p119/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · author | prefers | All five pronunciations are sound Arabic, but ṣād is preferred because every codex writes it that way and ṣād and ṭāʾ share emphatic articulation.
[THALABI:v1p119/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · رسول الله | reports | The Prophet identified the straight path as God's Book.
[THALABI:v1p119/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · عبد الله | reports | Ibn Masʿūd also glossed the straight path as God's Book.
[THALABI:v1p119/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · جابر | reports | Jābir calls the straight path Islam, wider than the space between heaven and earth, since other religions and paths are not straight.
[THALABI:v1p120/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · الحسن | reports | Al-Ḥasan affirms that Abū al-ʿĀliya spoke truth and gave sound counsel.
[THALABI:v1p120/r10] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو عثمان الداراني | reports | Abū ʿUthmān al-Dārānī glosses it as the path of servitude to God.
[THALABI:v1p120/r11] THALABI, d. 427 · سهل بن عبد الله التستري | reports | Sahl al-Tustarī calls it the path of Sunna and community, because innovation cannot

[THALABI:v1p120/r12] THALABI, d. 427 · رسول الله | reports | The Prophet drew one line for God's path and two side lines for other paths, each with a devil calling to it, then recited the command to follow God's straight path alone. | mentions 6:153
[THALABI:v1p120/r2] THALABI, d. 427 · بكر بن عبد الله المزني | reports | In a dream, the Prophet told Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allāh that the straight path is his Sunna and that of the rightly guided caliphs after him.
[THALABI:v1p120/r3] THALABI, d. 427 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿīd ibn Jubayr glosses the path as the way of truth.
[THALABI:v1p120/r4] THALABI, d. 427 · السدي | reports | Al-Suddī says it is the religion that brings its follower to Paradise without punishment and directly from the grave to Paradise.
[THALABI:v1p120/r5] THALABI, d. 427 · محمد بن الحنفية | reports | Muḥammad ibn al-Ḥanafiyya identifies it as God's religion, the only religion He accepts from servants.
[THALABI:v1p120/r6] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو بريدة | reports | Abū Burayda glosses it as the path of Muḥammad and his family.
[THALABI:v1p120/r7] THALABI, d. 427 · عبد العزيز بن يحيى | reports | ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz ibn Yaḥyā says it means the path of the great majority.
[THALABI:v1p120/r8] THALABI, d. 427 · أبو بكر الوراق | reports | Abū Bakr al-Warrāq defines it as a path whose directions are not bent right or left by whims.
[THALABI:v1p120/r9] THALABI, d. 427 · محمد بن علي النهدي | reports | Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī al-Nahdī calls it the path of fear and hope.
[THALABI:v1p121/r1] THALABI, d. 427 · رسول الله | reports | A prophetic parable identifies the straight path as Islam; its curtains are God's limits, open doors are His prohibitions, the caller on the path is the Qurʾān, and the caller above is God's inner adviser in each Muslim.
[MAWARDI:1:6/r1] MAWARDI, d. 450 · unattributed | reports | One interpretation of ihdina is guide us and show us the way.
[MAWARDI:1:6/r10] MAWARDI, d. 450 · النبي | reports | A report attributed to the Prophet likewise identifies the straight path as God’s Book; no grading is given.
[MAWARDI:1:6/r11] MAWARDI, d. 450 · جابر بن عبد الله ومحمد بن الحنفية | reports | Jabir ibn Abd Allah and Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya identify the straight path as Islam.
[MAWARDI:1:6/r12] MAWARDI, d. 450 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas identifies it as the way guiding to God’s religion, without any crookedness.
[MAWARDI:1:6/r13] MAWARDI, d. 450 · الحسن البصري وأبو العالية الرياحي | reports | Hasan al-Basri and Abu al-Aliya al-Riyahi identify the path as the Messenger and the best of his family and Companions.
[MAWARDI:1:6/r2] MAWARDI, d. 450 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn Abbas interprets ihdina as grant us success.
[MAWARDI:1:6/r3] MAWARDI, d. 450 · unattributed | reports | Sirat can mean the straight path, illustrated by Jarir’s verse about the commander being on a straight course when routes bend.
[MAWARDI:1:6/r4] MAWARDI, d. 450 · unattributed | reports | Sirat can also mean a clear road, as in 7:86 and the cited verse about turning from the clear path. | mentions 7:86
[MAWARDI:1:6/r5] MAWARDI, d. 450 · author | holds | Sirat derives from the passage of food as it moves through the throat.
[MAWARDI:1:6/r6] MAWARDI, d. 450 · unattributed | reports | The already guided ask for guidance to continue and remain constant.
[MAWARDI:1:6/r7] MAWARDI, d. 450 · unattributed | reports | Alternatively, the prayer asks God to increase their guidance.
[MAWARDI:1:6/r8] MAWARDI, d. 450 · unattributed | reports | A third view sees the request as sincere desire for guidance and hope for the reward of prayer.
[MAWARDI:1:6/r9] MAWARDI, d. 450 · علي وعبد الله | reports | Ali and Abdullah identify the straight path as God’s Book; a similar interpretation is attributed to the Prophet.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p58/r1] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Ihdina can mean guide and show us the way.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p58/r10] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن عباس | reports | He identifies it as the route that leads to God's religion and has no crookedness.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p58/r11] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · الحسن البصري وأبو العالية الرياحي | reports | They identify the straight path as the Messenger and the best of his family and Companions.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p58/r2] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · ابن عباس | reports | He interprets ihdina as grant us success in following the way.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p58/r3] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Sirat can mean the straight path, as illustrated by Jarir's verse.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p58/r4] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | Sirat can also mean the clear road; the Quran and another poem use it this way, and its root is the passage of food through the throat. | mentions 7:86
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p58/r5] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | The prayer for guidance can seek its continuation even for people already guided.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p58/r6] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | The prayer can ask God to increase their guidance.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p58/r7] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | The prayer can express sincere desire and hope for the reward of supplication.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p58/r8] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · علي وعبد الله | reports | They identify the straight path as God's Book; a similar interpretation is also transmitted from the Prophet.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p58/r9] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · جابر بن عبد الله ومحمد بن الحنفية | reports | They identify the straight path as Islam.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p518#2/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The term hādī broadened from a guide who leads by indication to any forerunner, including the leading animals, the neck, and a staff ahead of a traveler.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p518#2/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Poetic examples from ʿUbayd, Ṭarafa, and al-Aʿshā use guidance for leading, limbs that lead movement, and a staff that either precedes or directs its bearer.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p518#2/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The verb hadā takes two objects and connects the second with ilā or lām, as illustrated in 37:23, 38:22, 7:43, and 10:35; awḥā behaves similarly in 16:68 and 99:5. | mentions 37:23, 38:22, 7:43, 10:35, 16:68, 99:5
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p518#2/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The preposition before the second object can be omitted, as in 1:6; ihdinā al-ṣirāṭ means guide us to it and make us follow it. | mentions 1:6
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p518#2/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Already guided believers still ask because a knower may encounter doubts that lead back to ignorance, so they request a subtle divine aid that preserves knowledge.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p518#2/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | They also do not know their future state, so they ask for confirmation in the truth they presently follow; guidance can mean steadfastness rather than rescue from error.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p518#2/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | reports | Al-Ḥuṭayʾa's prayer that God guide ʿUmar is a wish for success and firmness, not a taunt that he is astray.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p518/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · الأصمعي | reports | Al-Aṣmaʿī says hadā-hu in religion means to guide him, while hadā-hu hidāya means to point someone to a road.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p518/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | The root meaning of guidance is indication; the leaders of horses and wild herds are called hawādī because they go in front to show the way.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p521/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · some of our companions | reports | Some scholars say believers ask for future guidance because guidance is an accident that does not endure, so they ask God to create its likeness anew.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p521/r10] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · صاحب الحجة | reports | The author of al-Ḥujja argues ṣād is preferable because sīn before emphatic ṭāʾ creates an unwanted rise in articulation, as speakers already replace sīn with ṣād before qāf.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p521/r11] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · صاحب الحجة | reports | Replacing sīn with ṣād is even more apt before ṭāʾ than before qāf because ṣād is closer to ṭāʾ.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p521/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · some scholars | reports | Others treat the prayer as claiming the fulfillment of God's promise in 5:16 to guide those who follow His pleasure toward paths of peace. | mentions 5:16
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p521/r3] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Ṣirāṭ has reported recitations with sīn, ṣād, zāy, and an intermediate ṣād-zāy pronunciation.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p521/r4] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · readers of sīn | reports | The sīn readers derive the word from istirāṭ, swallowing, because the road swallows travelers; they say a ṣād before ṭāʾ would hide the root.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p521/r5] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · readers of ṣād | reports | The ṣād readers say it is lighter and sounds better beside ṭāʾ because both are emphatic, unlike sīn, which is voiceless and farther from ṭāʾ.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p521/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · readers of zāy | reports | The zāy reading replaces sīn with a voiced sound, closer to ṭāʾ and light to articulate; they cite the Arab variant zaqr for ṣaqr.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p521/r7] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · readers of intermediate ṣād-zāy | reports | Those who blend ṣād and zāy seek ease without making either pure sound and thereby confusing the word's root.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p521/r8] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن السراج | prefers | Ibn al-Sarrāj prefers ṣād for ease, euphony, and clarity; it is also the majority recitation, while pure zāy is unrecognized and should not control recitation.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p521/r9] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · ابن السراج | rejects | He rejects the intermediate sound as a difficult, ad hoc articulation that is not an independent letter or a normal building block of words.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p528/r1] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · author | holds | Istiqāma means straightness and continuation along one direction: qāma is to stand upright, aqāma to straighten, and qāwama to match in strength.
[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p528/r2] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · علي وابن مسعود | reports | A report attri

[WAHIDI-BASIT:v1p528/r6] WAHIDI-BASIT, d. 468 · أهل المعاني | reports | The theologians of meaning say true religion is called the straight path because it reaches God's pleasure and lasting bliss, as a straight road reaches its destination.
[WAHIDI-QT:1:6/r1] WAHIDI-QT, d. 468 · author | holds | The prayer asks God to show the straight path, lead the petitioner along it, and keep him firm upon it.
[WAHIDI-WAJIZ:1:5-7/r3] WAHIDI-WAJIZ, d. 468 · author | holds | The prayer asks God to show the straight path, lead the worshippers along it, and keep them firm upon it.
[JURJANI-ASRAR:v1p47/r1] JURJANI-ASRAR, d. 471 · author | holds | The purest metaphor draws its likeness from intellectual images: the straight path denotes religion, while proof is light because its effect on the heart resembles light's effect on sight, without shared genus or bodily form. | mentions 7:157, 42:52
[DAMGHANI:v1p276/r12] DAMGHANI, d. 478 · author | holds | In the Fātiḥa, the straight path means the straight religion.
[JISHUMI:v1p213/r10] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | reports | Other proposed meanings ask for direction to Paradise in the Hereafter, future divine لطف to dispel doubts and satanic whispering even for believers, or direction to the route to success and deliverance.
[JISHUMI:v1p213/r11] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | prefers | The request to be kept on the path is best because it matches the preceding request for assistance.
[JISHUMI:v1p213/r3] JISHUMI, d. 494 · حمزة | reports | Ḥamza reads ṣirāṭ with an articulation between ṣād and zāy throughout the Qur’an.
[JISHUMI:v1p213/r4] JISHUMI, d. 494 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisāʾī is reported to articulate ṣirāṭ with an articulation between sīn and ṣād throughout the Qur’an.
[JISHUMI:v1p213/r5] JISHUMI, d. 494 · يعقوب برواية رويس | reports | Yaʿqūb in Ruways’s narration reads ṣirāṭ with sīn throughout the Qur’an; attribution of that reading to Ibn Kathīr is said to be mistaken.
[JISHUMI:v1p213/r6] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | prefers | The author prefers ṣād: it better harmonizes with emphatic ṭāʾ, is Qurashī, matches the written codex, and is the reading of most leading reciters; the other forms retain or suggest the root or harmonize voicing.
[JISHUMI:v1p213/r7] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | Guidance linguistically is indication or direction along a way, opposite error, and in essence indicates the truth; ṣirāṭ means path, from the image of swallowing food, and istiqāmah resembles evenness, opposite crookedness.
[JISHUMI:v1p213/r8] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | In ihdinā the object pronoun is the first object, ṣirāṭ the second, and al-mustaqīm modifies ṣirāṭ.
[JISHUMI:v1p213/r9] JISHUMI, d. 494 · أبي علي وأبي بن كعب | reports | One gloss asks God to keep the worshippers firm on the straight way of guidance, like telling someone already eating to continue eating.
[JISHUMI:v1p215/r1] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The verse requires asking God for guidance and teaches worshippers how to pray; it also calls for repeated supplication so desires do not lead them astray.
[JISHUMI:v1p215/r2] JISHUMI, d. 494 · author | holds | The author argues human acts are not created by God: otherwise requesting help and guidance would be pointless, like asking help for one’s colors or bodily form.
[BAGHAWI:1:6/r1] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · author | holds | Ihdinā means “guide us” or “direct us.”
[BAGHAWI:1:6/r10] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · سعيد بن جبير | reports | Saʿid ibn Jubayr says the straight path is the road to Paradise.
[BAGHAWI:1:6/r11] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · سهل بن عبد الله | reports | Sahl ibn ʿAbd Allah says it is the way of the Sunna and the community.
[BAGHAWI:1:6/r12] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · بكر بن عبد الله المزني | reports | Bakr ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Muzani says it is the way of God's Messenger.
[BAGHAWI:1:6/r13] BAGHAWI, d. 516 · أبو العالية والحسن | reports | Abu al-ʿAliya and al-Hasan identify it as the Messenger, his family, and his two Companions.

[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p629/r12] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | The twenty-third sense is correctness, as in asking whether a person is on the right guidance. | mentions 96:11
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p629/r13] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | The twenty-fourth sense is steadfastness: the prayer asks God to keep the worshippers on the straight path.
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p629/r2] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | A fourteenth sense is a messenger: the guidance sent to the Israelites and in Taha is glossed as a messenger. | mentions 2:38, 20:123
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p629/r4] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | The fifteenth sense is discernment, illustrated by the unbelievers who were not guided in their trade. | mentions 2:16
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p629/r5] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · قيل | reports | The sixteenth sense is a guide or indicator; in Moses's request, it can mean someone to show him the way to the fire if it is not actually fire. | mentions 20:10
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p629/r6] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | The seventeenth sense is teaching, as in God's teaching people the practices of those before them. | mentions 4:26
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p629/r7] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | The eighteenth sense is excellence or superiority: 'more guided' means better in way. | mentions 4:51
[IBNJAWZI-NUZHA:v1p629/r8] IBNJAWZI-NUZHA, d. 597 · author | holds | The nineteenth sense is leading or directing, as in driving people toward the path to Hell. | mentions 37:23

[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p14#2/r4] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · ابن عباس | reports | A fourth meaning is “inspire us,” likewise among the explanations transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās.

[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p14#2/r7] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · أبو عمرو والجمهور | reports | Abū ʿAmr and most readers use ṣād because it is lighter on the tongue.

[IBNJAWZI-ZAD:v1p14#2/r9] IBNJAWZI-ZAD, d. 597 · حمزة | reports | Two reports from Ḥamza describe blending sīn toward zāy, or pronouncing ṣirāṭ between ṣād and zāy.
[RAZI:1:1/r1] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi sketches the sūra’s sequence: seek refuge from sins, begin good works in God’s name, praise and recognize his lordship and mercy, heed judgment, worship and seek help, ask guidance, and avoid ignorance and error.
[RAZI:1:6/r1] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | The verse asks for guidance, which can be attained by seeking knowledge through proof and argument or by purifying the inner self through spiritual discipline.
[RAZI:1:6/r2] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Rational proofs are limitless because every atom in the upper and lower worlds testifies to God’s divinity, might and majestic self-sufficiency; the cited verse says each thing has a sign of His oneness.
[RAZI:1:6/r3] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | His proof starts from bodies equal in corporeal essence but different in color, place and condition; corporeality cannot explain this differentiation, so a specifying governor is required.
[RAZI:1:6/r4] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | If the specifying governor is a body, the same argument recurs; if not, the argument reaches its goal. If it acts by nature rather than knowledge and power, differentiation remains unexplained; a living, knowing, powerful agent is required.
[RAZI:1:6/r5] RAZI, d. 606 · ضياء الدين عمر | reports | Razi’s father says every individual atom contains infinitely many proofs of divine power, wisdom and mercy: it could occupy infinitely many positions and bear alternate attributes, each possible state showing dependence on its wise, merciful Creator.
[RAZI:1:6/r6] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Thus the rational route to guidance has no end; the alternative route is purification and spiritual discipline, an immense field with a distinct path for each traveler to God.
[RAZI:1:6/r7] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi says each traveler to God has a distinctive method and path, citing the Qur’anic statement that each has a direction toward which they turn. | mentions 2:148
[RAZI:1:6/r8] RAZI, d. 606 · author | holds | The intellect cannot master these spiritual secrets or their beginnings; accomplished knowers perceive profound discussions and subtle mysteries that most people’s understanding cannot reach.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p15/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The request is for guidance in every kind of guidance.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p152/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The straight path in belief avoids both excessive transcendence, which negates attributes, and excessive affirmation, which anthropomorphizes; it affirms without either error.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p152/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Regarding human acts, the middle position affirms human agency while holding that all occurs by God's decree, avoiding both Qadari determinism of human independence and denial of agency.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p152/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | In conduct, the straight path is moderation: chastity between indulgence and rigid abstinence, and courage between recklessness and cowardice.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p152/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعضهم | reports | Some say specifying the path of the favored shows that a seeker needs a guiding shaykh, since most people lack sound judgment and need a perfected guide's intellect.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p152/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi says the surah sets out the covenants of lordship and servitude together, as in God's promise to fulfill each side of His covenant. | mentions 2:40
[RAZI-FULL:v1p154/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The law, path, and reality complete human ascent: worship, reliance on God, and guidance culminate in fellowship with the pure and distance from the wretched.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p155/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | As the servant ceases serving rulers and relying on them for wealth or rank, he turns instead to worshipping God and seeking guidance and knowledge from Him.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p161/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أم سلمة عن النبي | reports | Umm Salama reports that the Prophet recited al-Fatiha while counting the basmala as its first verse, followed by the rest of its verses.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p162/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · أبو هريرة عن النبي | reports | In the divided-prayer report, God calls the basmala glorification, al-Hamd praise, the two mercy names extolling, the Master of Judgment entrustment, and the remaining response a sharing and a request granted.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p19/r13] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Asking for guidance has two routes: acquiring knowledge through proof and argument, and purifying the inner self through spiritual discipline.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p19/r14] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Proofs of God are inexhaustible because every particle in the upper and lower worlds testifies to divinity, majesty, and self-sufficiency.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p20/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The cited poem says every thing bears a sign of God's oneness; bodies share corporeality but differ in qualities, which requires a particularizing, wise agent rather than body or impersonal nature.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p20/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · ضياء الدين عمر | reports | Rāzī's father says each indivisible substance offers infinitely many proofs of power, wisdom, and mercy because it could occupy countless locations and bear countless possible attributes, each implying a wise, merciful maker.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p20/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Purification is an endless field, and each traveler to God has a distinct path and way; Rāzī cites the verse that each has a direction toward which they turn. | mentions 2:148
[RAZI-FULL:v1p20/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Human reason cannot reach the secrets of these spiritual paths, though realized knowers discern deep, subtle matters beyond most people's understanding.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p203/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The spiritual stations are knowledge of lordship and servitude; together they fulfill the covenant of 2:40. The opening praise establishes lordship, worship begins servitude, reliance completes it, and guidance is its fruit. | mentions 2:40
[RAZI-FULL:v1p205#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The apparent paradox is that a believer already has guidance; Rāzī answers that asking for the straight path can mean seeking the earlier believers' strength in bearing hardship for God.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p205#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Noah was beaten repeatedly and each time prayed for his people to be guided; Muhammad's repeated daily recitation of al-Fātiḥah means he uttered the request more often, so Noah's single prayer does not make him superior.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p205#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Guidance also means the just middle between excess and neglect in every character and action, including desire, anger, and spending; even a believer needs this balance. | mentions 2:143
[RAZI-FULL:v1p205#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A believer may know God through one proof yet overlook the many signs in created things; guidance asks God to reveal how each thing evidences His essence, attributes, power, and knowledge.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p205#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The straight path is wholehearted turning to God, as 42:52–53 and 6:153 say; it means following the prophets' endurance in sacrifice, obedience, exile, and even death, while the verse also offers the easier hope of repentance and accepted mercy. | mentions 42:52, 42:53, 6:153

item.text: The notes already show several separate questions: what “guide us” asks for, why guided people repeat the request, what the path denotes, and how its wording and readings work. I’m keeping those questions distinct while tracking notes that answer more than one.

mooth path out to Paradise.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p206/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · بعضهم | reports | Some identify the straight path as Islam, while others say it is the Qur'an.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p206/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | rejects | Rāzī rejects those identifications because the following apposition points to the path of earlier nations, who did not have the Qur'an and Islam; the intended path is that of the truthful and Paradise-worthy.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p206/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | “Path” rather than the synonyms way or road evokes the path to Hell, increasing fear and caution.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p206/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A second interpretation of “guide us” is “keep us firm in the guidance You have given,” as in 3:8; even learned people can be misled by a subtle doubt. | mentions 3:8
[RAZI-FULL:v1p206/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The plural prayer is more likely to be answered: if any Muslim merits a response, God's generosity will not answer some worshipers and reject the rest.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p207/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · رسول الله | reports | The Prophet says to call on God with tongues not used in sin; when the Companions ask who has such tongues, he tells them to pray for one another because none sinned with another's tongue.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p207/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The earlier wording “praise belongs to God,” rather than “I praise God,” includes all worshipers; the servant similarly says “guide us” to include them in his request.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p207/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · رسول الله | reports | The Prophet teaches that congregation is mercy and separation punishment; the servant therefore speaks collectively in praise, worship, reliance, guidance, following the righteous, and avoiding the condemned and astray, hoping to remain with the righteous in the next life. | mentions 4:69
[RAZI-FULL:v1p207/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Geometry defines a straight line as the shortest distance between two points; a weak servant asks for this shorter route.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p207/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | A straight road is uniquely recognizable, while crooked paths resemble and confuse one another, making the straight way safer.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p207/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The straight route reaches the goal, whereas a crooked route does not.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p207/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The straight route remains stable, whereas crooked paths change; this is the fourth reason to ask for it.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p214#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The seven Fatiha verses remove seven vices: praise dispels desire, Lord of the worlds greed, Judgment Day anger, worship and aid pride and vanity, guidance caprice, the favored path unbelief and doubt, and the final phrase innovation.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r11] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Human knowledge grows through one's own reasoning or through receiving predecessors' discoveries: “guide us” asks for the first, and the path of the favored for the second.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p215#2/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The effects of worship are guidance, unveiling, and disclosure, expressed in the request to be guided to the straight path.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Razi supports obligatory Fatiha recitation because the Prophet consistently recited it and commands require following him. | mentions 6:153
[RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r10] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The transmitted report itself says that prayer is not established without the Fatiha.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The rightly guided caliphs also consistently recited it, and the Prophet commanded Muslims to follow their sunna.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Muslims everywhere recite it in prayer, and the Qur'an commands following the path of believers. | mentions 4:115
[RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The prophetic statement “no prayer without the Opening of the Book” directly supports the requirement.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The command to recite what is easy from the Qur'an is obligatory; because reciting other passages is not, the obligatory recitation must be the Fatiha. | mentions 73:20
[RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Reciting the Fatiha is the safer course, following the prophetic instruction to leave what causes doubt for what does not.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The Prophet's constant practice makes abandoning his command forbidden, and Muslims agree that the Fatiha is better and more complete than another recitation. | mentions 24:63
[RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | If the superior prayer with the Fatiha discharges the obligation, it does not follow that the inferior prayer with another passage does; the obligation remains due.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p217#2/r9] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Prayer seeks remembrance of the heart, and this concise surah gathers lordship and servitude and is equated with the mighty Qur'an; nothing else can replace it. | mentions 20:14, 15:87
[RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · الله تعالى | reports | In a divine report transmitted by the Prophet, God responds to each Fatiha phrase: the opening remembers Him, praise praises Him, the mercy names magnify Him, Judgment Day glorifies Him or is entrusted to Him, worship belongs to Him, aid relies on Him, and guidance is the servant's request.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Calling the Fatiha “prayer” shows that religious law serves human interests: people most need knowledge of God's lordship and servitude, which the surah's two halves provide to fulfill the covenant. | mentions 17:7, 51:56, 76:2, 2:40
[RAZI-FULL:v1p217/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Since God names the Fatiha “prayer,” prayer without its recitation does not occur; Razi takes this to establish that reciting it is a pillar, as his school holds.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p219/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Scholars disagree about theology, prophecy, and resurrection despite comparable intellect and sustained inquiry; few reach the truth, so divine guidance must make truth attractive and falsehood repellent. | mentions 49:7
[RAZI-FULL:v1p219/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | People do not intend to believe falsehood; if choice alone controlled belief, no one would err, yet most go astray, showing that reaching truth depends on God's guidance.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p219/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Angels and prophets likewise attribute knowledge and guidance to God: Razi cites the angels, Adam, Abraham, Joseph, Moses, and Muhammad as examples. | mentions 2:32, 7:23, 6:77, 12:101, 20:25, 3:8
[RAZI-FULL:v1p219/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The seven Fatiha verses correspond to the seven bodily prayer acts—standing, bowing, rising, first prostration, rising between prostrations, second prostration, and sitting—as soul to body.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The request for guidance to the straight path corresponds to the second prostration, because the greatest request fits the greatest humility.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p220/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The seven Fatiha verses are the soul of the seven prayer acts, themselves the soul of seven stages of human formation; God is the soul of souls and light of lights. | mentions 23:12, 23:13, 23:14, 53:42
[RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · النبي | reports | A prophetic report says God has seventy veils of light; if unveiled, the splendor of His face would burn everything perceived by sight, and only prophetic light reveals the number.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r2] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Prayer was given to Muhammad as a gift for his community because it joins bodily ascent through actions with spiritual ascent through remembrances.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r3] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Before beginning the ascent, the worshipper purifies body and clothing for the holy presence and chooses which of opposing companions—angel or devil, reason or desire, truth or falsehood, and so forth—to follow, since settled companionship is hard to break. | mentions 9:119

[RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r6] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | “Blessed is Your name” unveils pre-eternity and eternity, since blessing here indicates abiding beyond extinction and nonexistence.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | “Exalted is Your majesty” signifies that God's knowledge and greatness exceed every stated measure.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p221#2/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | “There is no god but You” means every attribute of majesty and perfection belongs only to God; ultimately reason, speech, understanding, and imagination fail before Him.
[RAZI-FULL:v1p221/r1] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | Muhammad's ascent has a bodily journey from Mecca to Jerusalem and then the high kingdom, and a spiritual journey from the visible to the unseen and from the unseen to the unseen of the unseen. | mentions 53:9

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p48/r2] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | On al-Ḥasan’s and al-Ḍaḥḥāk’s reading, “the path of those” is a definite apposition to an indefinite, like “a straight path, God’s path.” | mentions 43:52
[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p48/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | On al-Ṣādiq’s and the majority’s readings, “the path of those” is an apposition of one definite to another, clarifying the previously somewhat vague “straight path.”

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v1p54/r3] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · author | holds | The shift to direct address in “You alone we worship,” “You alone we seek help,” and “guide us” is iltifāt.

[SAMIN-DURR:1:6#2/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ihd has pattern ifʿ, with its final weak yāʾ deleted by analogy to the jussive, where a weak final letter drops.

[SAMIN-DURR:1:6#2/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Hidāya can mean guidance, direction, or going ahead, as in the forelocks of horses; Imruʾ al-Qays uses the latter sense.

[SAMIN-DURR:1:6#2/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Another reported sense is supplication or calling, while deriving it here from inclination is mistaken because that belongs to a different root. | mentions 13:7, 7:56
[SAMIN-DURR:1:6#2/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · الراغب | reports | Al-Rāghib defines guidance as gentle indication; hadaytu is for directing, while ahdaytu is for giving a gift.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:6#2/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Al-ṣirāṭ is a readily traversed road, though some omit the qualification of ease; cited lines simply attest the road sense.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:6#2/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ṣirāṭ derives from swallowing: either the traveler swallows the road or the road swallows the traveler; this also explains calling it a mouthful or something that swallows.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:6#2/r9] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | reports | The original consonant is sīn; Qunbul reads it, while the common ṣād is an assimilation near the emphatic sound, as in cited lexical parallels.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:6/r1] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Ihdinā is an imperative form used here as a supplication; a command from superior to inferior is an order, the reverse a prayer, and one between equals a request.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:6/r2] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | The subject is obligatorily implicit anta; nā is the first object and a single attached pronoun form for first-person plural or royal first person across nominative, accusative, and genitive positions.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:6/r3] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The claim that yāʾ has the same one form across cases fails because nominative yāʾ addresses a woman, unlike the first-person yāʾ in accusative and genitive use.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:6/r4] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | Hum can look alike across cases, but nominative hum is detached while accusative and genitive hum are attached, unlike nā.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:6/r5] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Al-ṣirāṭ is the second object, and al-mustaqīm is its adjective, agreeing in the four relevant features.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:6/r6] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | holds | Hadā normally governs its first object directly and its second with ilā or lām; the preposition is omitted here, yielding direct government of both objects. | mentions 42:52, 17:9
[SAMIN-DURR:1:6/r7] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · البصريون | reports | Basrans hold that the imperative is indeclinable, whereas Kufans treat it as inflected.
[SAMIN-DURR:1:6/r8] SAMIN-DURR, d. 756 · author | rejects | The Kufan derivation of iḍrib from an imperative jussive with deleted lām and imperfect prefix is unnecessary; the author reserves a fuller refutation for a better place.

[BURHAN:v1p352/r1] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | holds | A good stop gives a complete sense, though what follows remains attached in wording or meaning and cannot be begun independently; the Fatiha examples illustrate it.

[ALUSI-FULL:v1p92/r11] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Another reported interpretation is turning away from everything besides God and devoting oneself wholly to Him.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p92/r2] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Ibn Kathir and Yaʿqub transmit the original sīn; most readers use the Qurayshi ṣād, Hamza colors ṣād toward zāy, and pure zāy is attributed to ʿUdhr and Kalb; Alusi judges ṣād most eloquent.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p92/r3] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Hijaz speakers treat ṣirāṭ as feminine, Tamim speakers as masculine; masculine use is more common, with plural patterns depending on gender.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p92/r4] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | holds | Al-mustaqīm is level and without crookedness.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p92/r5] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | One reported interpretation identifies the straight path as the true path.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p92/r6] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Other reported interpretations identify it with Islam or the Qur'an.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p92/r7] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · الرازي | rejects | Al-Razi rejects the Islam and Qur'an readings because the people blessed in 1:7 include earlier nations who had neither; Alusi objects that al-Razi elsewhere defines the path by universal moral moderation. | mentions 1:7, 2:143
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p92/r8] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · author | reports | A reported view makes the path knowledge of how each thing points to the divine essence and attributes.
[ALUSI-FULL:v1p92/r9] ALUSI-FULL, d. 1270 · قيل | reports | Another view makes it the early peoples’ path of enduring great hardships for God's pleasure.
[ELMALILI:1:5#9/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | After the covenant, the prayer for guidance begins as the most comprehensive practical application of seeking divine aid; it answers the worshipper's need, after pausing at “we seek aid,” to know where and how to begin.
[ELMALILI:1:5#9/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Guidance is contained in seeking aid, which is contained in worship and praise; thus all of Fatiha unfolds as one complete الحمد لله sentence and unified discourse, so its first two pauses are complete but not obligatory.
[ELMALILI:1:6#2/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Qur'anic rhetoric includes at least sixteen theoretically established categorical modes; suggestive, non-categorical rhetorical nuances are grasped through rhetoric's innumerable aesthetic judgments.
[ELMALILI:1:6#2/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Lexically the term means a straight, level highway, but the discourse concerns seeking aid, an immaterial matter, so it must mean a spiritual road or explicitly include one figuratively.
[ELMALILI:1:6#2/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The metaphor first imagines a clear, broad, busy, straight physical road, then a clear and comprehensive God-appointed intellectual and practical law safely directing human thought and action toward good goals, and finally uses “straight path” for that spiritual reality, clarified by “guide us.”
[ELMALILI:1:6#2/r12] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Whether every path that qualifies generally as a path of truth belongs to the requested straight path remains a question requiring consideration.
[ELMALILI:1:6#2/r13] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Because the preceding plea seeks aid, the first and most important request is guidance to a clear path that elicits divine aid; the passage therefore asks for God's most important assistance first.
[ELMALILI:1:6#2/r14] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Truth's broad meaning can encompass paths that lead to evil relative to created aims: each divine law leads to an objective, and some paths lead to God's pleasure while others lead to His wrath.
[ELMALILI:1:6#2/r15] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The requested path must therefore be defined as the path leading to God's pleasure; “the straight path” conveys a more specific and clearer meaning than the broad notion of a path of truth, and its appositional expansion identifies it fully with Islam.
[ELMALILI:1:6#2/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Chance is only an appearance to the ignorant; divine wisdom has no chance, and every choice by the all-wise has a weighting wisdom even though God's will is not externally compelled.
[ELMALILI:1:6#2/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | To interpret Qur'anic wording, establish each word's sense, compare related alternatives, consider syntax and context, then distinguish intended meaning from rhetorical embellishment; separate a term's mental sense from its real referents, since this affects legal inference.
[ELMALILI:1:6#2/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | Commentators transmit definitions including God's path, truth, a balanced way, God's Book, faith and its entailments, Islam and its law, the Prophet's and leading Companions' path, Sunna and the community, Paradise's road, and the bridge over Hell; investigators synthesize truth's path and Islam.
[ELMALILI:1:6#2/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Given the definite article's covenant or generic force, most transmitted explanations concern referents and some concern the concept; aside from Hell's brid

ge, they describe the same referent by attributes, so confusing sense with referent creates false disagreements.
[ELMALILI:1:6#2/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | prefers | The investigators' synthesis distinguishes concept from referent: “path of truth” gives the concept and Islam gives its real-world instance.
[ELMALILI:1:6#2/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The second mention of “path” explains the first by apposition, which can be whole or partial; the intended focus remains the apposition, while the first phrase prepares and reinforces the meaning rather than being discarded.
[ELMALILI:1:6#2/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The following appositional clauses clarify the path's essence and attributes: those whom God favored, those not under anger, and those not astray.
[ELMALILI:1:6#2/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The full appositional construction must be considered before the intended meaning and referent of the straight path can be determined.
[ELMALILI:1:6#3/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Because God is Lord of all worlds, His laws operate in every realm; laws may be named for their maker or their subject, but “divine laws” and “God's way” are more accurate for all of them.
[ELMALILI:1:6#3/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Knowing divine laws is science; laws that lead to good are religion, community, or sharia. Seeking religion outside divine ordinance is false, yet not every divine law is religion: the law that a suicide dies is real, but suicide is evil; good-conforming acts are religious, evil-conforming ones contrary to religion.
[ELMALILI:1:6#3/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Human-made laws cannot constitute true science or religion; people should discover and reveal God's laws rather than legislate them. Archimedes, Newton, Aristotle, and Abu Hanifa discovered laws rather than inventing them.
[ELMALILI:1:6#3/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Since divinely established laws are straight, “straight path” also conveys a clear, busy main road for revealing hidden laws and avoiding crooked human inventions unrelated to divine aid.
[ELMALILI:1:6#3/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Guidance's orientation to good does not erase the laws that lead to evil; it frames good laws positively as commands and evil laws negatively as prohibitions, and the following verse's favored/not-angered/not-astray clauses show both aspects. | mentions 1:7
[ELMALILI:1:6#3/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | With the definite article marking the covenant path, verse 6 is a complete definition of the true religion and the following material explains it. | mentions 1:7
[ELMALILI:1:6#4/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | In'am means giving and conveying a blessing; connecting it with “ala” conveys the Benefactor's exaltedness and the blessing's loftiness.
[ELMALILI:1:6#4/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Liberty cannot coherently belong to someone who rejects God or serves another; its guarantee lies in worshipping God alone. The straight path begins in servitude to God, aims first at the great worldly blessing of liberty, rests on life and faith, and depends on divine aid and guidance.
[ELMALILI:1:6#4/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Ni'ma first means a pleasurable state or bliss and then anything that causes it; it relates to softness. A proverb says some have wealth but no enjoyment, like someone with bread who cannot taste it; true blessing includes the ability to enjoy.
[ELMALILI:1:6#4/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | God's blessings cannot be counted; they may broadly be considered as worldly or afterlife blessings. | mentions 14:34, 16:18
[ELMALILI:1:6#4/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Worldly blessings are bestowed or acquired: bestowed gifts include spiritual and bodily capacities, while acquired gifts include moral purification, knowledge, virtue, social standing, and wealth.
[ELMALILI:1:6#4/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Afterlife blessings include forgiveness, attaining God's pleasure, and eternal repose in the highest station with the nearest angels; they too divide into bestowed/acquired and spiritual/physical forms.
[ELMALILI:1:6#4/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | An apparent present blessing may later become a calamity, and an apparent hardship may become happiness; real happiness is what ends safely, so the request is for blessings that bring a safe outcome rather than immediate pleasure.
[ELMALILI:1:6#4/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The qualification that excludes anger and misguidance restricts the potentially all-inclusive favor to lasting good: afterlife blessings and their worldly precursors, especially life, liberty, faith, sound conscience, good character, social rectitude, beneficial knowledge, and righteous action.
[ELMALILI:1:6#4/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | In Islamic usage, liberty means owning one's rights, as explained in Kashf al-Pazdawi; its opposite is enslavement through another's ownership of those rights.
[ELMALILI:1:6#4/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Rights originate in divine ordinance; if human law can alter or control them without consent, a person is partly enslaved and duties depend on another's arbitrary will rather than right.
[ELMALILI:1:6/r1] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The command form becomes an imperative from higher to lower, a supplication from lower to higher, and a request between equals.
[ELMALILI:1:6/r10] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The contextual setting determines which sense of guidance a Qur'anic occurrence carries.
[ELMALILI:1:6/r11] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | The verb may take its second object directly, as here, or with ilā; some grammarians explain the direct form as eliding the preposition for arrival, from an underlying “guide us to the path.”
[ELMALILI:1:6/r12] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Guidance and being guided are related; those already guided ask for steadfastness or a higher degree, while the previously unled ask to attain the basic guidance.
[ELMALILI:1:6/r13] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | The definite article on “the path” may mark a known covenant path belonging to God, or the generic class of road that metaphorically applies to God's path.
[ELMALILI:1:6/r14] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | reports | Most readings use ṣād as the Quraysh form, smoother and more eloquent due to emphatic sounds; Qunbul from Ibn Kathir and Ruways from Yaqub transmit sīn, while Hamza's ishmām hints at zāy in the Qays dialect (as Abu Hayyan reports).
[ELMALILI:1:6/r15] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Although Arabic “sirat” means a great, busy highway, Turkish speakers know it as the required afterlife bridge over Hell; the text hints at that image and Amr ibn Ubayd transmitted that interpretation, but exegetes take its primary intent as a representative metaphor for truth and Islam.
[ELMALILI:1:6/r16] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Arabic terms distinguish general road (tarīq), traveled road (sabīl), and busy, straight, great, or clear ways (including sirat and sharia); “sirat” therefore evokes sharia.
[ELMALILI:1:6/r17] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Mustaqim means completely straight with no bend; because a road may still slope, the adjective adds flatness, so “straight” alone does not fully convey it, though Turkish also uses it for true or truthful.
[ELMALILI:1:6/r2] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Guidance gently and delicately indicates how to reach a desired destination: it may show the way, take someone along it, or lead them all the way; showing is non-arriving direction (irshad), while taking there is tawfiq.
[ELMALILI:1:6/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Guidance concerns a good goal and gentle method; applying it to an evil destination, as in the direction to Hell, is figurative sarcasm or insinuation. | mentions 37:23
[ELMALILI:1:6/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | prefers | The best Turkish rendering is the familiar “bize hidâyet et”: “show” omits leading, “take” omits gentleness, and replacing an established word with a strained alternative distorts the intended meaning.
[ELMALILI:1:6/r5] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | Divine guidance is innumerable in both its particular forms and its kinds, but can be considered under four ordered general categories.
[ELMALILI:1:6/r6] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | One kind is bestowing and sustaining spiritual or bodily powers, senses, reason, will, and the natural or animal faculties that serve human needs, and aligning intentions with desires.
[ELMALILI:1:6/r7] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | A second kind establishes proofs that distinguish truth from falsehood and right conduct from corruption; the Thamud were shown guidance but preferred blindness. | mentions 90:10, 41:17
[ELMALILI:1:6/r8] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | A third kind guides through sending messengers and revealing scriptures, as with divinely guided leaders and the Qur'an's guidance to the soundest way. | mentions 21:73, 17:9
[ELMALILI:1:6/r9] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | A fourth, special guidance unveils hidden realities to hearts through revelation, inspiration, or true dreams, especially for prophets and saints; others have a limited share below certainty, and guidance can also be summarized as inner or outer, creational or revealed.
[ELMALILI:v1p85/r3] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | He seeks refuge in God's grace and guidance and asks for mercy because he has failed to worship adequately.
[ELMALILI:v1p85/r4] ELMALILI, d. 1361 · author | holds | He asks not to be led astray and asks God to enable right speech, to reveal divine joy, and to teach truth.

B-ZILAL, d. 1386 · رسول الله [ ص ] | reports | The Prophet says prayer is invalid without reciting the Opening of the Book; the report is in both Sahih collections.
[QUTB-ZILAL:1:1/r3] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | The short surah gathers core Islamic creed, worldview, feelings, and guidance, explaining its repetition in every rakʿa and why prayer without it is invalid.
[QUTB-ZILAL:1:6/r1] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | The prayer asks God both to show the connected, straight road and to keep the worshippers upright on it; knowing and following it are gifts of His guidance and care.
[QUTB-ZILAL:1:6/r2] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · author | holds | Guidance to the straight path is the believer's greatest and first request because it certainly secures happiness in both worlds and aligns human nature with God's law and creation.
[QUTB-ZILAL:1:7/r2] QUTB-ZILAL, d. 1386 · رسول الله | reports | Abu Hurayra reports in Sahih Muslim that God calls al-Fatiha a prayer divided between Himself and His servant: praise, mercy, and glorification are the Lord's; worship and aid are shared; guidance and the servant's request belong to the servant, who receives what he asks.
[IBNASHUR:1:2/r4] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Asking for guidance expresses a desire for sound judgment and admits one's need for knowledge.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r1] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | After praise, the worshipers' confession of exclusive worship and help bridges praise to petition; trusting God's welcome and hoping for His favor, they ask for guidance.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r10] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | rejects | He rejects that distinction as, at most, a prevalent usage rather than proof that the verb changes meaning with its construction; both huda and hidaya are verbal nouns, while the source noun is hady.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r11] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Hadā necessarily takes one object; for a second, it is direct when it means showing or clarifying, and prepositional when it means general guidance or pointing, so construction signals the embedded sense.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r12] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The basic sense is showing someone the route to a destination; guidance meanings developed as widely used metaphors from this literal sense.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r13] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | reports | The migration report says Abū Bakr hired a skilled route guide from Banū al-Dayl, illustrating the literal Arabic sense of hādī.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r14] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | In religious usage when ascribed to God, guidance is direction toward deeds pleasing to Him; its opposite, misguidance, is leading someone astray.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r15] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · الجمهور | prefers | The majority, including the Ashʿarites, define guidance as showing the way to an end whether or not arrival occurs; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls this correct.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r16] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · جماعة منهم الزمخشري | reports | A group including al-Zamakhsharī requires successful delivery in the definition, lest guidance fail to differ from misguidance; their dispute reflects different accounts of divine command and will versus creation.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r17] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | There is no dispute that guidance culminating in arrival is what religiously should be sought from both guide and guided, though a guide may err or the recipient may reject it.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r18] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · عبد الحكيم | reports | ʿAbd al-Ḥakīm chooses a shared sense covering both outcomes because the Qur'an uses guidance for each; absent contrary evidence, neither homonymy nor metaphor is assumed. | mentions 28:56, 41:17
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r19] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Guidance comprises four ordered kinds: innate powers for human existence, rational proofs distinguishing truth, revealed messengers and books for harder matters, and disclosure of higher truths.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r2] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The petition is the purpose of the preface, like the subject of a speech or the transition in a poem, fitting the Fātiḥa as a preamble to a book sent as guidance and mercy.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r20] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The first kind gives sensory and motor powers, from an infant's instinctive feeding and responses to danger through practical needs and the rational power that derives unknowns from knowns.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r21] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The second kind is theoretical knowledge supplied by proofs that distinguish truth from falsehood and correctness from error.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r22] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The third kind comes through messengers, revealed books, and measures of justice for matters beyond proof or too burdensome to settle by proof, as in God's description of the messengers. | mentions 21:73
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r23] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The highest kind unveils higher realities and meanings beyond the reach of rational minds through revelation, sound inspiration, or divine manifestations. | mentions 6:90
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r24] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | What a particular supplicant seeks depends on that person's or group's condition; as a prayer taught to all Quran-addressed believers, it requests kinds of guidance distributed according to each person's capacity.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r25] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Some guidance is sought for acquisition by those who lack it, while guidance already possessed, including much of the innate first kind, is sought for its continuance.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r26] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | A request form ordinarily asks that an act or abstention occur; asking only for continuance is figurative, as in the address to believers in 4:136. | mentions 4:136
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r27] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Asking for more guidance remains literal when some levels are attained and others lack; seeking increase also entails asking that existing guidance endure, making the request a kināya for continuance as well.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r28] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | For the Prophet, who had reached guidance's highest degree, the wording is figurative and an appropriation of the verse; the verse itself asks for complete guidance through further attainment and continuance.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r29] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Ṣirāṭ means a road; Arabic dialects pronounce it with ṣād or sīn, while the Hijaz dialect uses ṣād, an emphatic substitution easing the transition into emphatic ṭā.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r3] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · صاحب الكشاف | rejects | Al-Zamakhsharī treats the petition as an answer to an unstated question; Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers to read it as the natural aim of the preceding praise and confession.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r30] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · الجعبري | reports | Al-Jaʿbarī says Arabs change sīn to ṣād before several consonants; here ṣād matches ṭā in emphasis and elevation, avoiding a difficult movement from low articulation to high.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r31] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · حمزة | reports | Qays pronounces an intermediate sound between sīn and ṣād, called ishām, which Ḥamza reads in the transmission of Khalaf; al-Qurṭubī reports a pure zāy dialect among ʿUdhra, Kalb, and Banū al-Qayn, but says it is weak and unread.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r32] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · ابن كثير في رواية قنبل | reports | Most canonical readers use the eloquent ṣād form, while Ibn Kathīr in Qunbul's transmission reads sīn; Ibn ʿĀshūr prefers ṣād for its conformity to the muṣḥaf spelling and the eloquent dialect.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r33] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The Companions wrote ṣād to mark the more eloquent form in Quraysh usage; readers of sīn understood the written form as allowing known dialectal alternation, so the difference concerns pronunciation, not the word's lexical substance.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r34] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The spelling of al-muṣayṭir with ṣād likewise preserves a form whose origin is sīn, illustrating how the written ṣād need not rule out sīn pronunciation.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r35] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Al-ṣirāṭ is an Arabic word, although al-Naqqāsh and Ibn al-Jawzī report it as the Roman word for road; Abū Ḥātim is also cited, and al-Suyūṭī consequently listed it among loanwords.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r36] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The road is a metaphor for truth, through which a person reaches the success of God's approval that Islam seeks.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r37] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Mustaqīm is the active participle of istiqāma, the result of making something straight; it means having no bend or detour.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r38] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | A straight road is best because it reaches the destination most directly, without leading its traveller astray, causing hesitation, or producing confusion.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r39] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | By metaphor, the straight path is clear truth unmixed with false suspicion, like a road without branching side tracks.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r4] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The petition is separated from the preceding clauses because those clauses are declarative while this one is imperative.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r40] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · ابن عباس | reports | Ibn ʿAbbās explains the straight path as the true religion and is also reported to call it the religion of Islam; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the two glosses explain one another.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r41] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | Ibn ʿAbbās's gloss does not mean asking for an obsolete religion: all divinely revealed religions were straight paths for their own communities, as Satan's words about God's path also show. | mentions 7:16
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r42] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The definite article evokes a mentally understood kind, requested through its unique instance: straightness is singular, while misguidance has many forms. | mentions 10:32, 5:100
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r43] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | reports | One possible reading takes the path as Islam: God

[IBNASHUR:1:6/r45] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | prefers | He prefers that the path mean all sound knowledge, beliefs, and deeds: enabling people to recognize truth and distinguish it from error according to their capacities, without deviation or religious doubts.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r46] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | This reading is preferable because people need guidance in every affair, including preserving existing goodness from deficiency or deviation; guidance to Islam continues through its revealed and inferred laws, not only initial acceptance.
[IBNASHUR:1:6/r47] IBNASHUR, d. 1393 · author | holds | The comprehensive reading makes the transition to the following request, for the path excluding those under anger or astray, apt to the context.
